units.title: The American Revolution
units.blurb: Thirteen colonies, the quarrel over taxes, the Declaration of Independence, the war, and what the new nation set out to be.

parts.title: Thirteen Colonies
more: Harvard Classics: The First Step Toward Independence
ask: Name some of the thirteen colonies. Which one is closest to where we live?
How was life different in New England, the Middle Colonies and the South?
Colonists governed many of their own affairs for over a century. How might that have made them less willing to accept rules from far away?
parts.do: Draw the Atlantic coast on a long strip of paper and label the thirteen colonies from north to south. Keep it on the wall for the whole unit.

parts.title: Taxes and Protest
ask: What were the colonists upset about?
'No taxation without representation.' What did that mean?
Britain had spent a great deal defending the colonies in the French and Indian War. How might a British leader have seen the taxes differently from a colonist?
parts.do: Stage a two-sided family debate: one side speaks for Parliament, the other for the colonists. Then switch sides.

parts.title: The Declaration of Independence
more: Harvard Classics: Some Chose to Remain British Subjects
ask: What day do we celebrate the Declaration, and how?
Read the line about 'unalienable rights.' Which rights does it name?
Many signers held people in slavery while writing that all men are created equal. How did Americans later use those same words to argue for freedom?
parts.do: Read the Declaration's second paragraph aloud together. Each person copies one sentence in their best handwriting and signs their name below it.

parts.title: The War
ask: Who was George Washington, and what was his job in the war?
How could a new army beat Britain, which had one of the strongest armies in the world?
Many colonists stayed loyal to Britain. What reasons might a Loyalist family have had?
parts.do: Make a timeline on the wall from 1754 to 1783. Each person adds three events with dates and a small drawing.

parts.title: A New Nation
more: Harvard Classics: Washington's Dictum on Private Life
ask: After the war, the states needed rules for working together. What is a constitution?
Why did the Articles of Confederation not work well?
What changed for different groups of Americans after the Revolution, and what stayed the same?
parts.do: Write a family constitution: a short preamble saying what the family wants, and three rules everyone agrees to. Everyone signs.

parts.title: Symbols of the New Nation
ask: What do the stars and stripes on the flag stand for?
Why do countries have symbols at all?
The anthem was written in a later war, in 1814. Why might a young country need songs and symbols to hold it together?
parts.do: Learn the first verse of the national anthem together and talk through the hard words. Then fold a flag the traditional way.

A.do: Make a Liberty Bell from a paper cup or cardboard, with the crack. Tell the family what the bell stands for.
rubric: The bell is finished and shows the crack
Says what the bell stands for

B.do: Make a one-page newspaper from 1776 with a headline about the Declaration, a short news story, a drawing and an advertisement of the time.
rubric: Headline and story about a real event
Drawing and advertisement fit the time

C.do: Write two letters, one from a Patriot and one from a Loyalist, each explaining their choice to a friend. Use real events from the unit.
rubric: Uses at least three real events

D.do: Write a 2-3 page analysis of the Declaration as an argument: its premises, its evidence (the list of grievances) and its conclusion. How well does it persuade, and to whom was it written?
rubric: Lays out the argument's structure clearly
Quotes the text and explains each quotation

units.title: Ancient Egypt
units.blurb: The Nile and its flood, pharaohs and pyramids, gods and the afterlife, daily life, hieroglyphs, and how Egypt was found again.

parts.title: The Gift of the Nile
more: Herodotus: In the Cradle of Civilization
ask: Why did almost everyone in Egypt live close to the river?
The flood came every year. Why was it good news for farmers, and what happened when it was too low?
Herodotus called Egypt the gift of the Nile. Is that fair to the Egyptians who dug the canals and farmed the land?
parts.do: Make a Nile in a baking pan: a strip of soil down the middle, sand on both sides. Pour water along the soil and watch where it goes. Then plant a few seeds in the wet strip and check them each day this unit.

parts.title: Pharaohs and the Two Lands
ask: What did a pharaoh wear, and what did the two crowns stand for?
Egypt had pharaohs for about 3,000 years. What helped one kingdom last so long?
Egyptians said the king kept maat, the right order of things. How did that idea help a king rule, and what did it ask of him?
parts.do: Make a red crown and a white crown from paper, then fit them together into the double crown. Take turns telling one fact about a pharaoh while wearing it.

parts.title: Pyramids
ask: What shape is a pyramid, and what was inside one?
How did pyramids change from Djoser's steps to the smooth sides at Giza?
What do the workers' towns near Giza tell us about who built the pyramids, and what don't we know yet?
parts.do: Build a step pyramid from sugar cubes or blocks, then a smooth one. Count the blocks in each and talk about how many people a real one would need.

parts.title: Gods and the Afterlife
ask: Why did many Egyptian gods have animal heads?
Why did Egyptians take such care of the body after death?
In the weighing of the heart, what did a person's heart have to show? What does that tell us about what Egyptians valued?
parts.do: Draw a scale on a big sheet. On one side put a feather; on the other, write good deeds the family can do this week. Add one each day.

parts.title: Daily Life by the River
ask: What did Egyptian children eat and play?
Which jobs did Egypt need, and which do we still have today?
Most of what we know comes from tombs and the town of the tomb builders. How might that give us a lopsided picture?
parts.do: Cook a simple Egyptian-style meal together: flat bread, lentils, onions and dates. Play a board game of the time with a homemade board (a row-and-square race game like senet).

parts.title: Hieroglyphs and the Rosetta Stone
ask: How did a scribe write, and on what?
Some signs stand for sounds and some for ideas. Why would a writing system use both?
Champollion read hieroglyphs in 1822, after centuries when no one could. What did he need to know, and why did the Rosetta Stone matter so much?
parts.do: Write each family member's name in a cartouche using the sound signs, and hang them on the door. Then try to read each other's.

A.do: Make a four-page book: the river, a pharaoh, a pyramid and your name in hieroglyphs. Draw each page and tell a grown-up one sentence to write under it.
rubric: Each picture shows something real from the unit
Can tell one fact about each page

B.t: A day in an Egyptian village
B.do: Write a short story (one page) about a child in a farming village during the flood. Include a job, a meal, a game and one god the family honored. Add a drawing.
rubric: Story has a beginning, middle and end
At least four true details from the unit
Neat writing with capitals and end marks
A drawing that matches the story

C.do: Choose five things from ancient Egypt (a crown, a canopic jar, a scarab, a papyrus, a statue). Draw or model each and write a museum label: what it is, when it was made, what it was for.
rubric: Five objects, each drawn or modeled
Labels give name, period and use
Labels are clear and spelled correctly

D.t: How do we know? A short research paper
D.do: Write a 2-3 page paper on one question, such as how Egyptologists date the reign of a king, or what the workers' town tells us about the pyramid builders. Use at least three sources and cite them.
rubric: Evidence from at least three sources, cited
Separates what is known from what is guessed

units.title: Ancient Greece
units.blurb: Myths and heroes, Homer's Odyssey, Sparta and Athens, the Persian Wars, Greek art and buildings, and the Greek words we still use.

parts.title: Gods, Myths and Heroes
read: Famous Men of Greece: The Gods of Greece
ask: Which Greek god or hero did you like best, and why?
Greek myths often explain something in nature. Which one did, and what did it explain?
Heroes like Hercules are strong but not always good. What did the Greeks seem to admire in a hero?
parts.do: Find Greece on a globe or map, with its many islands and the sea all around. Then act out one myth together, with simple props.

parts.title: Homer and the Odyssey
read: Famous Men of Greece: The Adventures of Ulysses (I)
more: Harvard Classics: Odysseus Silenced the Sirens
Harvard Classics: Trapped in a Cave with a Frenzied Giant
ask: How did Ulysses trick the Cyclops?
Ulysses is clever more than strong. Where did his cleverness help him, and where did it get him into trouble?
Why might a story about a long trip home matter so much to people who lived by the sea?
parts.do: Make a map of Ulysses' trip home on a big sheet: draw each adventure as a stop. Add a stop each day as the story goes on.

parts.title: Sparta and Athens
more: Famous Men of Greece: Draco and Solon
ask: How was growing up in Sparta different from growing up in Athens?
Solon wrote laws for Athens. What makes a law fair?
Athens let many citizens vote but left out women, enslaved people and foreigners. How should we judge a people who began an idea but did not carry it all the way?
parts.do: Hold a family assembly the Athenian way: one question (what to cook Saturday), speeches for each side, then a vote with pebbles in two jars.

parts.title: Marathon and Thermopylae
read: Famous Men of Greece: Miltiades, the Hero of Marathon
more: Famous Men of Greece: Leonidas at Thermopylae
Harvard Classics: Citizens Lured from Their Homes
ask: Why did the small Greek cities fight the huge Persian Empire?
Why do we still call a long race a marathon?
The Greeks won by working together, then Athens and Sparta fought each other. Why is it hard for allies to stay friends after a war?
parts.do: Measure out a short 'marathon' course in your yard or a park and time each person. Then work out how many of your laps make 26 miles.

parts.title: Greek Art and Buildings
more: Harvard Classics: Athenians Also Complained of Taxes
ask: What pictures did the Greeks paint on their pots?
Find a column on a building near you. Is it plain, scrolled or leafy, like a Greek order?
Greek statues grew more lifelike over time. What changed, and why might artists have wanted that?
parts.do: Draw a Greek vase shape on orange paper and paint a scene from your own family's week on it in black, the way Greek painters showed everyday life and myths.

parts.title: Thinkers and Alexander
more: Famous Men of Greece: Alexander the Great
Harvard Classics: An Honest Life's Reward
ask: Socrates taught by asking questions. What is a good question to ask about something everyone thinks they know?
Alexander built a huge empire very fast. Why did it split apart after he died?
Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living. What do you think he meant, and do you agree?
parts.do: Play the question game at dinner: one person states something everyone believes, and the others may only ask questions, never argue, for five minutes.

A.do: Make a paper-plate mask of a Greek god or hero and tell the family that hero's story while wearing it.
rubric: The mask shows who the hero is (a tool or symbol)
Tells the story with a beginning, middle and end

B.do: Draw a six-panel comic of one adventure from the Odyssey, with speech bubbles and a caption for each panel.
rubric: Six panels in the right order
Characters and places match the story

C.t: Athens or Sparta? A comparison chart and speech
C.do: Make a chart comparing Athens and Sparta (government, schooling, army, daily life). Then give a two-minute speech on which city you would rather have grown up in, and why.
rubric: At least four points of comparison
Speaks clearly and keeps to time

D.do: Write a short dialogue (2-3 pages) in which Socrates questions someone about a big word such as courage, fairness or friendship. Show how the questions test each answer.
rubric: The question is clear from the start
Each answer is tested by a fair question
The reasoning is easy to follow
Ends with what was learned, even if the question stays open

units.title: Ancient Rome
units.blurb: Romulus and the early kings, the Republic, roads and aqueducts, Caesar and Augustus, Pompeii, and the Latin under our own words.

parts.title: The Founding of Rome
read: Famous Men of Rome: Romulus, part 1
ask: Who were Romulus and Remus, and what does the story say happened to them as babies?
Rome was built on seven hills by a river. Why was that a good place for a city?
Romans told this story about their own beginning. What does it say about how they wanted to see themselves?
parts.do: Find Italy on a map: the boot, the Tiber River and Rome. Then build seven hills from clay or play dough and set a small city among them.

parts.title: The Republic
more: Famous Men of Rome: Junius Brutus
Harvard Classics: Refused to Serve Three Terms
ask: Cincinnatus went back to his farm after he saved Rome. Why do people still admire that?
The Romans had two consuls instead of one king. Why would they want two?
George Washington was called a modern Cincinnatus. Which choices of his fit that name?
parts.do: Make a family Senate: elect two 'consuls' for the week who share one job (choosing the read-aloud time). At the end of the week, they give it up.

parts.title: Roads, Aqueducts and Arches
read: Famous Men of Rome: Appius Claudius, part 1
ask: How did Romans bring water into their city?
Why does an arch hold up so much weight?
Roman roads helped trade and travel, and also moved armies. Can a good invention serve both peace and war?
parts.do: Build an arch from sugar cubes or blocks over a curved support, then take the support away. Try it without a keystone and see what happens.

parts.title: Hannibal and the Punic Wars
read: Famous Men of Rome: Scipio Africanus, part 1
ask: How did Hannibal get his army and elephants over the Alps?
Rome lost big battles to Hannibal but still won the war. How?
Regulus kept a promise to his enemies even though it cost him his life. Was he right?
parts.do: On a big map of the Mediterranean, trace Hannibal's march from Spain over the Alps into Italy. Measure it with the map scale.

parts.title: Caesar and Augustus
read: Famous Men of Rome: Julius Caesar, part 2
more: Harvard Classics: Beware the Ides of March!
Famous Men of Rome: Augustus, part 2
ask: What does 'crossing the Rubicon' mean today?
The months July and August are named for Julius Caesar and Augustus. Why would the Romans honor them that way?
Rome went from a republic to rule by an emperor. Why might citizens accept losing some of their say in exchange for peace?
parts.do: Make a calendar page for July and August with Roman numerals for the dates. Practice reading the numerals out loud.

parts.title: Pompeii and the End of the West
read: Harvard Classics: Survivor's Story of Vesuvius
more: Famous Men of Rome: The end of the Western Empire
ask: What happened to the town of Pompeii in AD 79?
Pliny wrote a letter about what he saw. Why is an eyewitness letter so useful to historians?
Historians still argue about why the Western Empire fell. Which causes seem strongest to you, and what would you need to know to be sure?
parts.do: Make a volcano from a bottle, clay and baking soda with vinegar. Then talk about why ash buried the town so quickly and kept it for us to find.

A.do: Decorate a cardboard shield with an eagle or another Roman symbol and the Roman numerals for your age. Show it and tell one thing about Rome.
rubric: The shield has a Roman symbol
The Roman numeral for your age is right
Tells one true thing about Rome

B.do: Build a model of an arch, a road in layers, or an aqueduct that carries water downhill. Write five sentences on how it works.
rubric: The model works or shows the idea clearly
Uses at least two words from the unit (arch, keystone, aqueduct)

C.do: Write a letter, as a Roman child, to a cousin far away. Describe one big event (Hannibal's march, Caesar crossing the Rubicon, Vesuvius) as if you saw it.
rubric: Includes three real details of Roman life

D.t: Why did the Western Empire fall? A short essay
D.do: Write a 2-3 page essay weighing three causes historians give for the fall of the Western Empire. Say which you find strongest and why, and give the other views fairly.

units.title: Citizenship
units.blurb: Rules and helpers, rights and duties, voting, local government, how someone becomes a citizen, and serving the community.

parts.title: Rules and Helpers
ask: Who helps keep our town running?
What would happen if nobody followed the rules of the road?
Is it ever right to break a rule? What would make it right?
parts.do: Visit or write to a community helper (a librarian, a mail carrier, a firefighter). Ask what their job is like, and thank them.

parts.title: Rights and Responsibilities
ask: What does a good citizen do?
What rights do citizens have, and what do they owe in return?
Which matters more to a free country, rights or duties? Can you have one without the other?
parts.do: Make a family chart of rights and responsibilities: for each right in the home (to be heard, to have your things respected), write the matching duty.

parts.title: Voting
ask: How do we choose leaders in our country?
Why is a vote secret?
Why do some eligible people not vote? What could change that?
parts.do: Hold a secret-ballot family election on something real (the next family outing). Make ballots, a ballot box and count the votes together.

parts.title: Our Town and State
read: Local Government in Civics and Government
ask: Who is in charge of our town?
What does a city council or county board decide?
Some decisions are made in town, some in the state capital and some in Washington. Why not make them all in one place?
parts.do: Attend a town council or school board meeting together (or watch one online). Write down one decision made and how it was made.

parts.title: Becoming a Citizen
ask: How do people become citizens of the United States?
Try five questions from the citizenship test. Which were hardest?
Why does the country ask new citizens to learn its history and government?
parts.do: Take a practice citizenship test as a family, with older children asking the questions. Talk about what surprised you.

parts.title: Serving Others
read: Heroes of Service: Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King Jr.
ask: How can kids help their neighbors?
Rosa Parks and Dr. King changed laws by peaceful protest. How did that work?
What is the difference between charity and changing a law? Does a community need both?
parts.do: Plan and do a family service project: rake a neighbor's leaves, collect food for a pantry, or make cards for a nursing home.

A.do: Make a card for a community helper with a drawing of them at work. Deliver it together.
rubric: A drawing of the helper's job

B.do: Make a small handbook: five rights, five responsibilities, how voting works, and who leads your town and state.
rubric: Real names of local and state leaders

C.do: Pick a question your town is deciding (a park, a road, a school rule). Interview two people with different views and write a fair one-page report on both sides.
rubric: No side taken unless asked; clear writing

D.do: Plan and lead a community service project with the family. Write a 2-page report: the need, your plan, what happened, and what you would do differently.

units.title: Ecosystems
units.blurb: Habitats, food chains and webs, decomposers, predators and prey, biomes, and how living things change their surroundings.

parts.title: Habitats
ask: What does an animal need from its home?
Why can't a polar bear live in a desert?
What happens to the animals when a habitat changes quickly?
parts.do: Explore a square yard of ground (a hula hoop works). Count every living thing you find inside it, and draw a map of it.

parts.title: Food Chains
ask: What did you eat for lunch, and where did its energy first come from?
Draw a food chain with four links. What happens if one link disappears?
Why are there always fewer big predators than plant eaters?
parts.do: Make a food chain paper chain: each link is one living thing, starting with the Sun. Then join chains together into a web on the wall.

parts.title: Decomposers
more: Nature Study: Field observations on ants
ask: What happens to a leaf after it falls?
Why are worms and mushrooms important to a forest?
Where would all the dead plants and animals be if there were no decomposers?
parts.do: Make a compost jar: layers of soil, leaves, fruit peels and a few worms. Keep it damp and dark, and look each week.

parts.title: Predators and Prey
ask: Name a predator and its prey.
How do prey animals stay safe? Think of colors, speed and herds.
In the simulation, why do the numbers of rabbits and foxes rise and fall in turns?
parts.do: Play a predator-and-prey tag game in the yard: a few 'foxes' and many 'rabbits.' Count both after each round and graph them.

parts.title: Biomes of the World
ask: What is it like in a rainforest? In a desert?
Which biome do we live in? How can you tell?
Why are biomes found in bands around the world?
parts.do: Make a biome box (a shoebox scene) of a biome you would like to visit, with its plants, animals and weather.

parts.title: People and Nature
ask: How can our family take care of the living things around us?
How do people change ecosystems, for good and for harm?
People disagree about how to balance using land with protecting it. What are the main concerns on each side?
parts.do: Do one thing for local wildlife: hang a bird feeder, plant a native flower, or pick up litter at a park. Keep a log of the visitors.

A.do: Make a hanging mobile of a food chain: the Sun at the top, then a plant, a plant eater and a meat eater. Tell the family how energy moves down it.

B.do: Survey one small area outside three times. List the living things you find, draw five of them, and make a food web from what you found.
rubric: A food web with arrows the right way

C.do: Make a travel guide to one biome: climate (with a climograph), plants, animals, a food web, and how people use it.
rubric: Plants and animals that really live there

D.do: Use the Predators and Prey simulation to run three experiments (change one setting each time). Graph the populations and write a report explaining the patterns with what you learned about ecology.
rubric: Says what a real ecosystem adds that the model leaves out

units.title: Fables and Folk Tales
units.blurb: Aesop's fables and their morals, animal characters, tales from McGuffey's Readers, Grimm and Andersen, and writing your own fable.

parts.title: What Is a Fable?
read: Harvard Classics: 2,500 Years Ago Aesop Said . . .
ask: What happened to Androcles and the lion?
What is the moral, the lesson, of the story?
Why might a teacher tell a story instead of just saying the lesson?
parts.do: Start a family fable jar: each person writes or draws one moral (a lesson in a sentence) on a slip and puts it in. Each night, pull one and tell a fable that fits.

parts.title: Animal Characters
read: McGuffey's Second Reader: The Fox and the Ducks
ask: Why is the fox in so many fables?
Which animal stands for which kind of person: the fox, the ant, the lion?
Animals in fables stand for people. Why might that make a lesson easier to hear?
parts.do: Draw animal masks for a fox, a crow and a lion. Act out 'The Fox and the Crow' from memory, then switch masks.

parts.title: Fables About Honesty
ask: Why didn't anyone come the last time the boy cried 'Wolf!'?
Once trust is lost, how can someone earn it back?
Is it ever right to tell a lie? What do the main traditions of thought say?
parts.do: Play two truths and a lie at dinner, then talk about how it felt to be fooled, even in a game.

parts.title: Folk Tales from Grimm
read: Harvard Classics: A Flounder Fish Story (Grimm)
more: Harvard Classics: Old Stories Ever New (The Valiant Little Tailor)
ask: What did the fisherman's wife keep asking for?
Why do so many folk tales repeat things three times?
The brothers Grimm wrote down stories people told aloud. What might change when a spoken story is written down?
parts.do: Tell a folk tale around the table, one sentence each, going around and around. Record it, then listen back.

parts.title: Andersen's Tales
read: Harvard Classics: World's Greatest Bedtime Stories (The Ugly Duckling)
more: Harvard Classics: The Night Life of Flowers (Little Ida's Flowers)
ask: How did the ugly duckling feel, and how did it end?
How is a fairy tale different from a fable?
Andersen was teased as a child. Do you think the story is about him? What makes you think so?
parts.do: Draw the duckling's year as a four-panel strip: spring, summer, autumn and winter, then spring again.

parts.title: Write Your Own Fable
read: McGuffey's Fourth Reader: Waste not, Want not
ask: What lesson would you like to teach with a story?
Which animals would make good characters for your lesson?
A good moral is short and surprising. How do you keep a fable from preaching?
parts.do: Fable-writing night: everyone writes or dictates a fable. Read them aloud and guess each moral before it is told.

A.do: Make two paper-bag puppets and act out a fable for the family. Say the moral at the end.
rubric: Two puppets that fit the fable

B.do: Write and draw three fables of your own, each with animal characters and a moral at the end.
rubric: Animal characters that stand for something

C.do: Find three fables or folk tales from different countries that teach a similar lesson. Retell each briefly and write a page comparing them.

D.do: Write a 2-3 page essay on one Grimm or Andersen tale: its structure, its symbols and what it says about the time it came from. Support every claim with the text.
rubric: Evidence from the text with quotations
Considers the time and place of the tale

units.title: Famous Paintings
units.blurb: How to look at a painting, then the Renaissance, the Dutch masters, the Impressionists and American painters, with color and design along the way.

parts.title: How to Look at a Painting
more: Formal analysis in Art History I
ask: What is the first thing you notice in this painting?
Where does the painting lead your eye, and how?
Can you enjoy a painting without knowing its story? What does knowing the story add?
parts.do: Pick one painting from the gallery. Look at it in silence for two minutes, then take turns naming one thing each until no one can find anything new.

parts.title: The Renaissance
read: Leonardo da Vinci in Art History I
more: Linear perspective in Art History I
ask: What is the woman in the Mona Lisa doing with her face?
How did Renaissance painters make flat walls look deep?
Leonardo was a painter, an engineer and a scientist. Did one help the others?
parts.do: Try Leonardo's soft shading (sfumato): draw a ball with only light pencil strokes, blending with a finger so no edge shows.

parts.title: The Dutch Masters
ask: What is happening in Vermeer's quiet rooms?
Where does the light come from in a Vermeer? In a Rembrandt?
Why might a nation of merchants want paintings of everyday life instead of kings and saints?
parts.do: Set up a still life on a table by a window: a jug, some fruit, a cloth. Draw or paint it, paying attention to where the light falls.

parts.title: The Impressionists
more: Monet's series in Art History II
ask: What colors do you see in Monet's water lilies?
Why did the Impressionists paint outdoors, quickly?
Critics first laughed at Impressionism. Why do new styles so often meet scorn before they are admired?
parts.do: Paint the same view from a window three times in one day: morning, noon and late afternoon, as Monet did with his haystacks.

parts.title: American Painters
read: The Hudson River School in Art History II
more: Early America in Art History II
ask: What do these painters love about the American land?
Why did painters in the 1800s paint such huge, wild landscapes?
How might these paintings have shaped what Americans thought about the West?
parts.do: Paint or draw a landscape from a real place near you: the sky, the far hills or buildings, and something close up in front.

parts.title: Color and Design in Paintings
ask: Which painting from this unit has the happiest colors? The saddest?
How do painters use color to point your eye to the most important part?
Does color mean the same thing in every culture? How could you find out?
parts.do: Make a family art gallery: each person frames their best work from the unit and writes a small museum label. Invite someone to visit.

A.do: Pick a painting from the unit and make your own picture in the same colors or the same subject. Show both side by side.
rubric: Uses colors or a subject from the master's painting

B.do: Make a book with one page each for five painters from the unit: a sketch of one of their paintings, their name, when they lived and one thing about their style.
rubric: Style described in your own words

C.do: Choose four paintings from the unit. Write and record a one-minute audio guide for each: what to look at, how it was made and why it matters.

D.do: Write a 2-3 page formal analysis of one painting: line, color, light, composition and subject, then what the choices mean in their time.
rubric: Interpretation supported by what is visible

units.title: Fractions in the Kitchen
units.blurb: Halves and quarters, measuring cups, doubling and halving recipes, ratios, percents on labels and planning a week of meals, cooking from the Meal Prep recipes.

parts.title: Halves, Thirds and Quarters
ask: If we cut a pizza into four equal pieces, what is each piece called?
Which is bigger, one half or one quarter? Why does the bigger number give the smaller piece?
Can two halves be different shapes and still be halves?
parts.do: Make the sheet-pan pizza together and cut it into halves, then quarters, then eighths, naming each fraction as you go.

parts.title: Measuring Cups and Spoons
more: Meal Prep: Pancake mix from scratch
ask: Which cup is bigger, the 1/2 cup or the 1/3 cup?
How can you measure 3/4 cup with only a 1/4 cup?
How many tablespoons are in a cup, and how could you figure it out with water?
parts.do: Make pancakes from scratch. Let each child measure one ingredient, saying its fraction out loud, and check with a different cup.

parts.title: Doubling and Halving a Recipe
ask: If the recipe makes 12 muffins and we want 24, what do we do?
What is half of 3/4 cup? How about double 2/3 cup?
Some things don't scale simply, like baking time or a single egg. Why not?
parts.do: Bake banana muffins at one and a half times the recipe. Write the new amount for every ingredient before you start.

parts.title: Ratios and Recipes
ask: For every cup of oats we use one cup of milk. What if we use three cups of oats?
A salad dressing is 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar. How much of each makes one cup?
Why do bakers often weigh ingredients and think in ratios instead of cups?
parts.do: Make overnight oats in jars, one per person, with each jar the same ratio but a different size. Check that they taste the same.

parts.title: Percents on the Label
ask: Find a number with a % sign on a box in the pantry. What does it mean?
If a serving is 1/4 of the box, how many servings are in the box?
Labels use a 'daily value' based on a typical diet. Why might that number fit some people better than others?
parts.do: Read five labels from the pantry together. Line them up by serving size and by one number you choose (like fiber), and make a chart.

parts.title: Planning a Week of Meals
ask: What should we have for dinner this week?
How much will the food for the week cost, and how can we spend less?
How do you plan meals that are healthy, cheap and quick, when those goals pull against each other?
parts.do: Plan a week of dinners together with the Meal Prep planner. Each child chooses one meal, makes the shopping list for it and helps cook it.

A.do: Make a snack plate cut into halves and quarters (a sandwich, an apple, a tortilla). Show the family each fraction and share it fairly.

B.do: Copy a family recipe neatly onto a card, then write a second card with every amount doubled and a third with every amount halved.

C.do: Choose a Meal Prep recipe, scale it to feed the family exactly, make the shopping list with prices, and cook it with a grown-up. Show your math on one page.
rubric: Shopping list with prices and a total
The meal is cooked and served

D.do: Compare three ways to make one dish (from scratch, from a mix, ready-made). Work out the cost per serving and time per serving, make a table and graph, and write up which you would choose and why.

units.title: Letter Writing
units.blurb: The parts of a letter, thank-you notes, friendly letters and pen pals, famous letters from history, business letters and email.

parts.title: The Parts of a Letter
ask: What goes at the top of a letter, and what goes at the end?
Why do we start with 'Dear' even when writing to a stranger?
A letter is slower than a text. When is slow better?
parts.do: Set up a family post office: a shoebox mailbox for each person. Everyone writes at least one short letter to someone in the house each day this week.

parts.title: Thank-You Notes
read: Thank-You Notes in Manners for Growing Up
ask: Who could you thank this week, and for what?
What makes a thank-you note feel real instead of polite?
Why does a handwritten note still matter when an email is faster?
parts.do: Each person writes or draws three thank-you notes to people who have helped the family. Address the envelopes and mail them together.

parts.title: Friendly Letters and Pen Pals
read: Harvard Classics: Letters to an Emperor (Pliny)
ask: What would you tell a pen pal about your life?
How do you make a letter sound like you?
Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan nearly 2,000 years ago, and we still have the replies. What do letters save that history books leave out?
parts.do: Find a pen pal (a cousin, a grandparent, a friend who moved away). Each person writes a first letter with three questions to answer back.

parts.title: Letters That Made History
read: Harvard Classics: Survivor's Story of Vesuvius (Pliny)
more: Harvard Classics: Columbus' Letter Miraculously Found
ask: What did Pliny see from across the bay?
Why do historians trust a letter written at the time more than a story told years later?
Columbus wrote his letter to win support back home. How might that shape what he chose to say?
parts.do: Write a letter to a grandparent or older friend asking about one thing they remember from when they were your age. Save the answer in a family history folder.

parts.title: Persuasive Letters
read: Harvard Classics: A Letter from a Lion (Johnson)
ask: If you wrote to the mayor, what would you ask for?
What reasons would make the mayor want to say yes?
Johnson's letter is polite and devastating at once. How does he manage both?
parts.do: Write a real letter of request: to a library asking for a book, to a park about a broken swing, or to a company about a product you like or dislike. Mail it.

parts.title: Email and Business Letters
ask: How is an email to Grandma different from an email to a teacher?
What makes a good subject line?
Why is it wise to read an email twice before sending it, especially when you're upset?
parts.do: Write a practice email to a pretend company asking a question. Trade with someone in the family, who answers it as the company.

A.t: A letter to someone far away
A.do: Draw a picture and dictate a short letter to a relative or friend who lives far away. Help address the envelope and put it in the mailbox.
rubric: Has a greeting and a closing

B.do: Write three letters to a pen pal over the unit, each with a greeting, three paragraphs or parts, and a closing. Keep copies in a folder with any replies.
rubric: Three complete letters in letter form
Capitals, commas and end marks correct

C.do: Write a polite, persuasive letter to a local leader (mayor, librarian, park director) about a real issue. Include a clear request, three reasons and a thank-you. Mail it.

D.do: Gather or transcribe five letters from your family's or your town's past (or from a public archive). Write a 2-page introduction explaining what they show about their time.
rubric: Each letter's date and writer identified
An introduction that draws careful conclusions

units.title: Logical Fallacies
units.blurb: What an argument is, giving reasons, attacking the person, the straw man, false choices and hasty conclusions, and arguing fairly.

parts.title: What Is an Argument?
ask: What is the difference between a quarrel and an argument?
Find the reason in this sentence: 'We should bring umbrellas because it is cloudy.'
Can an argument be good even if you disagree with its conclusion?
parts.do: At dinner, each person makes a claim about something small (the best fruit) and gives one reason. Others say whether the reason supports the claim.

parts.title: Attacking the Person
ask: If someone says 'You're wrong because you're little,' is that fair?
Why doesn't who says something decide whether it is true?
When is it fair to point out that a speaker has a reason to mislead?
parts.do: Fallacy detectives: a grown-up reads silly ads or made-up arguments, and the kids hold up a card when they hear someone attack the person instead of the reason.

parts.title: The Straw Man
ask: If I say 'I want a small snack' and you say 'You want to eat all the cookies!', is that what I said?
Why is it tempting to make the other side sound sillier than it is?
What does it take to state someone's view so well that they'd agree you got it right?
parts.do: Steelman game: one person states a view, and another must repeat it back so well that the first person says 'Yes, exactly.' Then switch.

parts.title: False Choices
ask: 'Either you like dogs or you hate animals.' Are those the only choices?
How can you spot an argument that leaves out other options?
Some choices really do have only two options. How do you tell a real either-or from a false one?
parts.do: Two-choice challenge: a grown-up gives five either-or statements, and the kids find a third option for each.

parts.title: Jumping to Conclusions
ask: If one cat scratched you, are all cats mean?
How many examples do you need before you can say 'always'?
Two things happen together. How can you tell if one caused the other?
parts.do: Flip a coin ten times and record the results. Does a run of heads mean the next flip will be tails? Try it a few times and see.

parts.title: Arguing Fairly
ask: How can we disagree and still be kind?
Which fallacy from this unit do you hear most often?
Is it fair to call out a fallacy in a friend's argument? How would you do it kindly?
parts.do: Hold a short family debate on a fun question (cats or dogs, summer or winter). Everyone must steelman the other side before they rebut.

A.do: Make a poster: 'I think ___ because ___' with three of your own opinions and a good reason for each. Draw a picture for each.
rubric: Each has a reason that fits

B.do: Draw a comic strip for four fallacies from the unit. Each strip shows a character making the mistake and another catching it.

C.do: Make a field guide to eight fallacies: name, a plain definition, an example you made up and a tip for spotting it.

D.do: Pick a famous speech or essay from before 2000 (the Gettysburg Address, a Federalist essay, a Lincoln-Douglas debate). Map its argument, name any fallacies, and write a 2-3 page evaluation that also states its strongest points fairly.
rubric: Fallacies named with evidence, not guessed

units.title: Maps and Mapmaking
units.blurb: What a map is, keys and symbols, directions and the compass, grids and coordinates, scale and distance, and the globe.

parts.title: What Is a Map?
ask: What does your room look like from above, like a bird would see it?
Why do maps leave things out?
Every map is drawn for a purpose. How does the purpose change what goes on it?
parts.do: Each person draws a bird's-eye map of their bedroom. Swap maps and try to find a hidden toy using someone else's map.

parts.title: Keys and Symbols
ask: What symbol would you use for a park? A school?
Why does every map need a key?
How can a map's colors and symbols make a place look better or worse than it is?
parts.do: Make a map of your neighborhood walk with your own symbols and a key. Take the walk and add anything you missed.

parts.title: Directions and the Compass
read: Home Geography: How the compass shows direction
ask: Where does the Sun come up in the morning?
How does a compass needle know where north is?
Why might a compass point a little away from true north?
parts.do: Hide a treasure and write directions in steps and compass directions (ten steps north, five east). Trade directions and hunt.

parts.title: Grids and Coordinates
ask: On a grid, how do you say exactly where a square is?
How do latitude and longitude make a grid for the whole Earth?
How does a phone know where it is on that grid?
parts.do: Play family battleship on graph paper with lettered columns and numbered rows. Then find your home's latitude and longitude.

parts.title: Scale and Distance
more: Home Geography: How to tell distance
ask: How can a whole town fit on one piece of paper?
If one inch on the map means one mile, how far is three inches?
A map can't show everything at every scale. What do you lose on a map of the whole world?
parts.do: Measure the yard or a room in paces or feet, then draw it to scale on graph paper (one square = one foot).

parts.title: The Globe and Flat Maps
ask: Why is a globe round?
Find the equator and the poles. Which part of the Earth is hottest?
Every flat map of the world stretches something. Why is Greenland so big on some maps?
parts.do: Peel an orange in one piece if you can, then try to lay the peel flat. Talk about why flat maps of a round world must stretch or tear.

A.do: Draw a map of your home or yard with a key of at least four symbols and a compass rose.
rubric: Can find three places on the map

B.do: Make a treasure map of your yard or a park with a grid, a key, a compass rose and a scale. Write five clues using grid squares and directions.
rubric: Grid, key, compass rose and scale
Someone can follow it to the treasure

C.do: Map a few blocks of your neighborhood to scale, with a key, a scale bar, a north arrow and real street names.
rubric: Measurements turned into a correct scale
Key, scale bar and north arrow

D.do: Collect data on a question (where your town's parks are, which states grow the most corn) and make a thematic map with a clear legend, a title and a short write-up on the pattern you see.
rubric: A suitable map type and clear legend
An honest write-up of the pattern

units.title: Matter and Chemistry Basics
units.blurb: Solids, liquids and gases, measuring matter, mixtures and solutions, atoms and elements, and changes you can see in the kitchen.

parts.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
read: Fairy-Land of Science: Solids, liquids, gases
ask: Is water a solid, a liquid or a gas? Can it be all three?
What happens to the tiny particles in ice as it melts?
Why does a gas fill any container you put it in, but a liquid doesn't?
parts.do: Freeze a cup of water and mark the top. When it's frozen, look again: did it grow or shrink? Then let it melt and boil a little in a pot with a grown-up, watching the steam.

parts.title: Measuring Matter
ask: Which is heavier, a cup of rice or a cup of popcorn?
Why do scientists all use the same units?
Why does a big log float but a small stone sinks?
parts.do: Density tower: in a tall clear glass, slowly pour honey, dish soap, water with food coloring and cooking oil. Drop in a grape, a coin and a cork and see where each stops.

parts.title: Mixtures and Solutions
ask: Where does sugar go when you stir it into water?
Can you get salt back out of salt water? How?
Why does more sugar dissolve in hot tea than in iced tea?
parts.do: Grow crystals: dissolve as much salt or sugar as you can in warm water, hang a string in it, and check it every day for a week.

parts.title: Atoms and Elements
ask: Everything is made of tiny pieces. What are they called?
What are an atom's three main parts?
How can just over a hundred elements make every substance in the world?
parts.do: Build atoms from candy or clay: one color for protons, one for neutrons, one for electrons. Make hydrogen, helium and carbon, and check them in Build an Atom.

parts.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
ask: When you bake a cake, can you get the eggs back out?
How can you tell that a new substance was made?
Is dissolving sugar a chemical change? Argue both sides, then decide.
parts.do: Mix baking soda and vinegar in a bottle with a balloon over the top. Watch the balloon fill, then talk about what gas was made.

parts.title: Chemistry in the Kitchen
read: The Chemical History of a Candle: What candles are made of
more: Acids and bases in the Chemistry Ladder
ask: Which foods taste sour? What makes them sour?
Why does a cut apple turn brown, and why does lemon juice slow it down?
Faraday gave his candle lectures to young people in 1860. Why did he think a candle could teach all of chemistry?
parts.do: Make a red cabbage indicator: chop red cabbage, soak it in hot water, and strain. Add a spoonful to lemon juice, vinegar, water, and baking soda water, and line up the colors.

A.do: Make a three-column poster with pictures (drawn or cut out) of solids, liquids and gases from your home. Tell the family about one in each column.
rubric: Each picture is in the right column

B.do: Grow crystals from two different solutions (salt and sugar). Measure and draw them every two days and write what was different.

C.do: Choose a kitchen experiment (cabbage indicator, baking soda reaction, density tower). Present it to the family with a poster explaining the science.
rubric: The poster explains the science correctly
Uses at least four science words correctly

D.do: Measure how much gas (by balloon size or mass lost) different amounts of baking soda make with the same vinegar. Find the limiting reactant and write a lab report with a graph.
rubric: Measurements with units and repeated trials
Correctly identifies and explains the limiting reactant

units.title: Measurement
units.blurb: Length, weight, capacity, time and temperature, measured around the house, with units, conversions and estimates.

parts.title: Length
ask: How many of your hands tall is the table?
Why did people stop measuring with hands and feet?
Why does the world mostly use meters, and why does the United States still use feet and inches?
parts.do: Measure the same table with hand spans, a shoe, a ruler and a tape measure. Compare everyone's hand-span answers and talk about why they differ.

parts.title: Weight and Mass
ask: Which is heavier, a pillow or a can of beans?
Big things are not always heavy. Why not?
What is the difference between mass and weight? Would you weigh the same on the Moon?
parts.do: Make a balance from a hanger and two cups. Compare pairs of things from the kitchen, then check with a kitchen scale.

parts.title: Capacity and Volume
ask: Which glass holds the most? Guess, then pour to check.
How many cups make a quart? A gallon?
A tall thin glass and a short wide one can hold the same amount. How can you prove it?
parts.do: Pouring station at the sink: cups, pints, quarts and a gallon jug. Find how many of each fill the next one, and make a chart.

parts.title: Time
read: Time to the Hour and Half Hour
more: Home Geography: How the sun shows direction
ask: What time do we eat breakfast? Lunch?
How much time passes from when school starts to lunch?
Before clocks, how did people tell time? Why did railroads need everyone's clocks to agree?
parts.do: Make a family daily schedule with clock faces drawn for each part of the day. Use a timer to guess and check how long chores really take.

parts.title: Temperature
ask: Is it hot or cold outside today? How can we know for sure?
What temperature does water freeze at? Boil at?
Why are there different temperature scales, and how do you change from one to another?
parts.do: Read a thermometer at the same time each day for a week, indoors and out. Graph both lines on the same chart.

parts.title: Estimating and Checking
ask: How many steps is it to the mailbox? Guess, then count.
When is a good estimate better than an exact answer?
Every measurement has some error. How do scientists show how sure they are?
parts.do: Estimation Olympics: everyone guesses the length, weight, volume and time of five things, then measures. Score how close each guess was.

A.do: Make a book called 'How big is it?' with five things you measured using blocks or hand spans, drawn and labeled.

B.do: Measure five rooms or things in feet and inches, a few things in cups and pounds, and how long three chores take. Present it as a chart.
rubric: At least ten measurements with units

C.do: Measure one floor of your home and draw it to scale on graph paper. Work out the area of each room and the whole floor.

D.do: Measure one quantity (the period of a pendulum, the length of a room, the density of a stone) ten times. Report the mean, the spread, the percent error against a known value, and how you could improve.

units.title: Money
units.blurb: Coins and bills, making change, what money is for, earning and choosing, saving and interest, and a family budget.

parts.title: Coins and Bills
ask: Which coin is worth the most? Is it the biggest one?
How many different ways can you make 25 cents?
Why is a dime smaller than a nickel but worth more?
parts.do: Empty a coin jar onto the table. Sort the coins, count each pile, and find the total together.

parts.title: Shopping and Making Change
ask: If something costs 60 cents and you pay a dollar, how much change do you get?
How do cashiers count up to make change?
Why do so many prices end in 99 cents?
parts.do: Set up a family store with price tags on toys and snacks. Take turns as shopkeeper and customer, paying with real coins and making change.

parts.title: What Money Is For
read: Harvard Classics: They Had No Money, Yet Bought and Sold
ask: What would it be like to trade without money?
Why did people start using coins?
Money is only worth something because people agree it is. How can that work?
parts.do: Hold a barter morning: everyone trades toys, books or snacks with no money. Then try again with play money, and talk about which was easier.

parts.title: Earning and Choosing
more: Harvard Classics: Wages, Why and How Much?
ask: How do grown-ups earn money?
If you spend your money on a toy, what else can't you buy?
Why are some jobs paid more than others? List the main reasons economists give.
parts.do: Make a family job board: small paid jobs beyond the usual chores. Each child chooses jobs and keeps a record of what they earn this week.

parts.title: Saving and Interest
read: Use a Bank Account (Being an Adult 101)
more: Harvard Classics: Franklin's Advice for the New Year
ask: What are you saving for?
How does a bank pay you for keeping money there?
Why does money saved early grow so much more than money saved later?
parts.do: Make three jars for each child: spend, save and give. Split this week's earnings among them and label each jar with a goal.

parts.title: A Family Budget
ask: What does our family spend money on?
What is the difference between a need and a want?
If prices rise and pay stays the same, what has to change in a budget?
parts.do: Give each child pretend money for a pretend month. They must pay for 'needs' cards, choose 'wants' cards, and keep a little for savings.

A.do: Make a book with a page for each coin and the dollar bill: a rubbing or drawing, its name and its value.
rubric: A page for each coin and the dollar
Can count a small handful of coins

B.do: Choose something to save for. Make a chart of what you earn and save each week, and figure out how many weeks until you reach your goal.
rubric: A clear goal with a price

C.t: Run a small business for a day
C.do: Plan a lemonade stand or bake sale: costs, prices, how many you need to sell to break even. Run it and write a one-page report on profit and what you learned.
rubric: A cost list and price plan

D.do: Build a monthly budget for a young adult living on their own in your area: a realistic job and pay after tax, rent, food, transportation, savings. Use a spreadsheet and real prices, and write a page on the hardest trade-offs.
rubric: Realistic income and costs, with sources

units.title: Perspective
units.blurb: Near and far, overlapping and size, the horizon line, one-point and two-point perspective, and the haze that makes distance.

parts.title: Near and Far
ask: Look out the window. Which things look small because they are far away?
How can a drawing on flat paper look deep?
Children's drawings often stack far things higher on the page. Is that wrong, or another way of showing space?
parts.do: Line up toy figures down a hallway and photograph them. Then draw what you see, making the far ones smaller.

parts.title: The Horizon Line
ask: Where does the sky meet the ground?
Why does the horizon move up when you stand on a chair?
Why does the horizon line always sit at the artist's eye level?
parts.do: Hold a ruler level at your eye, outdoors, and find the horizon. Then sit on the ground and stand on a step, and see how it moves.

parts.title: One-Point Perspective
more: Linear perspective in Art History I
ask: Stand in a long hallway. What happens to the walls as they go away?
Where do the lines of the road meet in a picture?
Brunelleschi showed this method around 1420. Why did it change painting so much?
parts.do: Draw a road or railroad going straight away from you to one point on the horizon. Add trees or poles that get smaller as they go.

parts.title: Boxes and Buildings
ask: How can you make a square look like a box?
Which edges of a box are parallel in real life but meet in a drawing?
Why might an architect draw a building in perspective before it is built?
parts.do: Collect boxes of different sizes. Arrange them on a table and draw them from a low eye level and then from above.

parts.title: Two-Point Perspective
ask: Look at the corner of a house. How many sides can you see?
Why does a corner view need two vanishing points?
When would an artist break the rules of perspective on purpose?
parts.do: Draw a street corner in two-point perspective, with two vanishing points on the edges of the page. Add windows and doors.

parts.title: Atmosphere and Distance
more: The Hudson River School in Art History II
ask: Why do far-away mountains look blue?
How can colors and edges show that something is far away?
Leonardo wrote about this haze. What did careful looking teach him that rules alone could not?
parts.do: On a hazy day (or in photos), compare the colors of near hills and far hills. Paint a landscape in four layers, each farther one lighter and bluer.

A.do: Draw a road going far away, with a house near and a house far, and color the sky and ground.
rubric: A near house bigger than the far one

B.do: Draw a street in one-point perspective with at least three buildings, trees or poles, and people at different distances.
rubric: Lines go to the vanishing point

C.do: Design your dream bedroom in one-point or two-point perspective, with furniture drawn as boxes and then finished in detail.

D.do: Draw one real building three ways: a straight-on view, a one-point view and a two-point view. Write a page on what each view shows best.

units.title: Plants and Seeds
units.blurb: What plants need, roots, stems and leaves, how plants make food, flowers and pollinators, seeds and how they travel, and the plants we eat.

parts.title: What Plants Need
more: Home Geography: What plants need to grow
ask: What does a plant need to live and grow?
How could we test whether a plant really needs light?
In a fair test, why do we change only one thing at a time?
parts.do: Start a bean test: plant beans in four cups. Give one cup no light, one no water, one no soil (wet paper towel), and one everything. Check them every day of the unit.

parts.title: Roots, Stems and Leaves
ask: What does each part of a plant do?
How does water get from the roots to the top of a tall tree?
Why do leaves have tiny openings, and what is the trade-off of having them?
parts.do: Put a white carnation or a celery stalk in water with food coloring. Check it after a few hours and again the next day, then cut the stem to look inside.

parts.title: How Plants Make Food
more: Fairy-Land of Science: How a plant makes its own food
ask: Where does a plant get its food?
What goes into a leaf, and what comes out, when it makes sugar?
Most of a tree's mass comes from the air, not the soil. How can that be?
parts.do: Cover part of a leaf on a living plant with foil for three or four days. Then compare its color with the uncovered part.

parts.title: Flowers and Pollinators
more: Fairy-Land of Science: Taking a flower apart
ask: Why do bees visit flowers?
What are the parts of a flower, and what does each do?
Why might a plant 'pay' a bee with nectar? What does each side get out of it?
parts.do: Take apart a large flower (a lily or tulip from the store works well). Lay out the parts on paper, label them, and look at the pollen with a magnifying glass.

parts.title: Seeds and How They Travel
more: Fairy-Land of Science: Inside a seed
ask: How do seeds get to new places?
Soak a bean overnight and open it. What is inside a seed?
Why might a plant make thousands of seeds when only a few will grow?
parts.do: Go on a seed hunt outside (or in the kitchen). Sort what you find by how it travels: wind, water, animals, or popping.

parts.title: Plants We Eat
ask: Which part of the plant is a carrot? A lettuce leaf? An apple?
Where in the world did corn, wheat and potatoes first come from?
Farmers have changed crops over thousands of years by choosing seeds. How is that like and unlike changing a plant's genes in a lab?
parts.do: Make a 'parts of the plant' salad or snack plate: roots (carrots), stems (celery), leaves (lettuce), flowers (broccoli), fruits (tomatoes) and seeds (sunflower seeds).

A.do: Draw your bean plant every two days in a little book. A grown-up writes down what you say about how it changed.

B.do: Write up the four-cup bean test: the question, what you did, a chart of heights by day, and what you found out.
rubric: States the question and the one thing changed
A conclusion that matches the results

C.do: Make a field guide to eight plants near your home: a drawing or pressed leaf, its name, where it grows, and how its seeds travel.

D.do: Plan and run an experiment on one plant growth factor (light color, salt in water, fertilizer amount). Write a lab report with hypothesis, method, data table, graph and conclusion.
rubric: A fair method with one variable changed and a control
Data in a table and a graph
A conclusion that discusses error and next steps

units.title: Poetry
units.blurb: Rhythm and rhyme, pictures in words, nature poems, story poems, poems about people, and writing and reciting your own.

parts.title: Rhythm and Rhyme
read: Home Geography: What the winds bring (poem)
ask: Which words in the poem rhyme?
Clap the beat of one line. Where do the strong beats fall?
Why do so many old poems rhyme, and why do many newer ones not?
parts.do: Rhyme chain: one person says a word, and everyone takes turns with a rhyme until someone gets stuck. Then clap the rhythm of a nursery rhyme.

parts.title: Pictures in Words
read: Harvard Classics: Nature Guided His Pen (Wordsworth)
ask: What picture did you see in your mind as you listened?
Find a simile (like or as) or a metaphor. What two things does it compare?
Why might a poet say something is something else instead of saying it plainly?
parts.do: Go outside for ten quiet minutes. Each person writes or says five 'picture' lines about what they see, hear and feel.

parts.title: Nature Poems
more: Harvard Classics: A Field Mouse Made Famous (Burns)
ask: What does the brook say about itself?
How does the poet make the sound of water in the words?
Burns wrote to a mouse whose nest he had plowed up. What larger point does he make about plans?
parts.do: Read the poem aloud as a family, each person taking a line, with sound effects (a pan of water, rustling paper). Record it.

parts.title: Story Poems
read: Harvard Classics: How the Glorious News was Carried to Aix (Browning)
more: Harvard Classics: O Captain! My Captain! (Whitman)
ask: What happens in the poem? Tell it back in order.
How does the rhythm sound like galloping horses?
Whitman never names Lincoln in 'O Captain! My Captain!' How do we know who it is about?
parts.do: Act out a story poem: one narrator, the rest acting it in mime. Swap parts and do it again.

parts.title: Poems About People
more: Harvard Classics: A Psalm of Life and other poems (Longfellow)
ask: Who is the poem about? What do we learn about them?
What words does the poet choose to show how the person feels?
Can a short poem tell us as much about a person as a long biography? Why or why not?
parts.do: Each person writes or dictates a short poem about another family member: three things they do and one thing they love. Read them at dinner.

parts.title: Writing and Reciting
ask: Which poem from this unit do you want to learn by heart?
What makes a poem easy to remember?
Why did people once learn so many poems by heart? Is it still worth doing?
parts.do: Hold a family poetry night: each person recites a poem from memory and reads one they wrote. Serve a special snack.

A.do: Learn a short poem by heart. Draw a picture for it, and say it for the family on poetry night.
rubric: A picture that fits the poem

B.do: Write four poems of your own (one rhyming, one about nature, one about a person, one of your choice). Copy them neatly into a little book with drawings.
rubric: At least one uses rhyme well

C.do: Collect ten favorite poems (from the unit and elsewhere) into an anthology. For each, write a short note on why you chose it and one thing the poet does well. Add two of your own.
rubric: Organized with a table of contents

D.do: Choose one poem from the unit. Write a 2-3 page close reading: what the poem says, how its sound, images and structure work, and what it means. Recite it on poetry night.
rubric: A clear thesis about the poem
Analysis of sound, imagery and structure with quotations

units.title: Simple Machines
units.blurb: Pushes and pulls, levers, wheels and axles, pulleys, ramps, wedges and screws, and how machines trade force for distance.

parts.title: Pushes and Pulls
ask: Is opening a door a push or a pull? What about a drawer?
Why is it harder to push a full wagon than an empty one?
What does it mean that every push comes with an equal push back?
parts.do: Go on a push-and-pull hunt around the house. Make two lists, then see which things need both.

parts.title: Levers
ask: How does a seesaw let a small child lift a bigger one?
Where is the fulcrum on scissors? On a bottle opener?
Archimedes said that with a long enough lever he could move the world. What did he mean?
parts.do: Make a lever from a ruler and a pencil. Stack coins on each end and move the pencil until they balance. Record where the fulcrum is for each pile.

parts.title: Wheels and Axles
ask: What would life be like without wheels?
Why is it easier to turn a doorknob than the thin rod inside it?
Why do big wheels roll over bumps more easily than small ones?
parts.do: Build a car from a box, two straws for axles and bottle caps for wheels. Roll it down a board and measure how far it goes.

parts.title: Pulleys
ask: How does a flag get to the top of a flagpole?
Why does a pulley with two wheels make lifting easier?
If a pulley halves the force, what do you give up in exchange?
parts.do: Hang a broom handle between two chairs. Loop a rope over it to lift a bucket of books, then add a second loop and feel the difference.

parts.title: Ramps, Wedges and Screws
ask: Why do ramps help people move heavy things?
How is an axe like a ramp?
A screw is a ramp wrapped around a pole. Why does that let it hold so tightly?
parts.do: Pull a toy truck full of coins up a board with a rubber band. Measure how far the band stretches as the ramp gets steeper.

parts.title: Machines in Our Lives
more: Harvard Classics: Pins and Other Points
ask: Find a machine at home made of two simple machines together.
A bicycle uses many simple machines. Which ones can you find?
Machines can't make energy. So how does a machine help us at all?
parts.do: Take apart something old and broken (a toy, a pencil sharpener, a clock) with a grown-up, and find every simple machine inside.

A.do: Draw five simple machines you found at home, one per page, and tell a grown-up what each one helps you do.
rubric: Each one is a real simple machine

B.t: Build a working lever or pulley
B.do: Build a lever or pulley that lifts a small load. Test it with three loads and write down what you found.
rubric: Explains how it makes lifting easier

C.do: Design and build a machine that uses at least three simple machines to do one small job (ring a bell, drop a ball in a cup). Draw a labeled plan.

D.do: Measure the force needed to lift a load directly, with a ramp and with a pulley. Calculate the ideal and actual mechanical advantage and the efficiency of each, and write a lab report.
rubric: Compares ideal and actual and explains the difference

units.title: The Civil War
units.blurb: Slavery and the road to war, Lincoln, the two sides, Gettysburg, emancipation, Clara Barton and the home front, and Reconstruction.

parts.title: Slavery and Freedom
ask: What does it mean to be free?
How did Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman work against slavery?
The Declaration said all men are created equal, yet slavery was legal in many states. How did abolitionists use the nation's own founding words?
parts.do: Read one short passage from Frederick Douglass's Narrative aloud (a grown-up chooses it first). Talk about why learning to read mattered so much to him.

parts.title: A House Divided
more: Harvard Classics: Oxford Corrects Lincoln's Mistake
ask: What was Abraham Lincoln like as a boy?
Why did Southern states leave the Union after Lincoln was elected in 1860?
Lincoln said a house divided against itself cannot stand. What did he mean, and was he right?
parts.do: Make a Lincoln log cabin from pretzel sticks or craft sticks. While you build, take turns telling stories from his life.

parts.title: Two Sides
read: Two Sides in U.S. History I
ask: Which states were in the Union and which in the Confederacy?
The North had more factories and railroads. Why didn't that end the war quickly?
Why did border states like Kentucky and Maryland matter so much to both sides?
parts.do: Color a map of the states in 1861: Union, Confederacy and border states. Count how many of each.

parts.title: Gettysburg
more: Harvard Classics: Gettysburg by an Eyewitness
ask: Why do we remember the battle of Gettysburg?
Lincoln's speech was very short. Which words stay with you?
Lincoln called the war a test of whether a nation 'conceived in liberty' could last. What did he think the soldiers had died for?
parts.do: Each person learns one or two sentences of the Gettysburg Address. Together, recite the whole speech in order.

parts.title: Emancipation and the Home Front
more: Harvard Classics: O Captain! My Captain!
ask: How did Clara Barton help soldiers?
What did the Emancipation Proclamation do, and what didn't it do?
How did the war change life for women, for freed people and for families at home?
parts.do: Put together a care package for someone who serves (a nursing home, a fire station, a neighbor in the military), and write a note to go with it.

parts.title: Reconstruction
ask: After the war, what did the country need to rebuild?
What did the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments promise?
Why did many of the promises of Reconstruction go unkept for so long, and how were they finally pursued?
parts.do: Make a 'promises' chart: the three amendments in one column, and in the other, when each promise was fully kept in practice. Fill it in as you read.

A.do: Draw a picture of Clara Barton or another helper from the unit and dictate a thank-you message to go with it.
rubric: Picture shows the helper and what they did
A message that says thank you and why

B.do: Make a timeline from 1850 to 1877 with at least eight events, each dated, with a sentence and a small picture.
rubric: At least eight events, correctly dated

C.t: A soldier's or nurse's letters home
C.do: Write three letters home from a soldier or nurse at different points in the war (1861, 1863, 1865). Use real places and events.
rubric: Three letters at three points in the war
Shows how the writer's view changes

D.t: The Gettysburg Address, line by line
D.do: Write a 2-3 page analysis of the Gettysburg Address: its occasion, its structure, its key words and its appeals. Compare it with Edward Everett's two-hour speech that day.
rubric: Analyzes structure and word choice with quotations

units.title: The Constitution
units.blurb: Why the Constitution was written, the three branches, checks and balances, the Bill of Rights, federalism, and how it can be changed.

parts.title: Why a Constitution?
more: Harvard Classics: Hamilton, Father of Wall Street
ask: What would a game be like with no rules?
What problems did the country have under the Articles of Confederation?
The Preamble begins 'We the People.' Why does it matter who a government says its power comes from?
parts.do: Read the Preamble aloud and act out each of its six goals (union, justice, peace at home, defense, welfare, liberty) as charades.

parts.title: Three Branches
ask: What are the three branches, and what does each one do?
Why split power three ways instead of giving it to one person?
Give an example of one branch checking another. Is there a risk in too many checks?
parts.do: Make a three-legged stool from cardboard and label each leg with a branch. Take one leg away and see what happens.

parts.title: Congress and How a Bill Becomes a Law
read: How a Bill Becomes a Law
ask: Who makes the laws for our country?
Why does Congress have two houses, one by population and one with two senators per state?
Most bills never become law. Is that a flaw, or did the framers mean it to be hard?
parts.do: Write a family 'bill' (a later bedtime on Fridays?). Pass it through two 'houses' (the kids and the grown-ups) and a 'president' who may sign or veto.

parts.title: The Bill of Rights
read: The Bill of Rights in U.S. History I
ask: What is a right? Name one right you have.
Why did some states refuse to ratify the Constitution until a bill of rights was promised?
Rights sometimes pull against each other or against public safety. How should a free country decide where one right ends?
parts.do: Make a poster of the first ten amendments in your own words, one short line each, with a small drawing for each.

parts.title: States and the Nation
ask: What is the capital of our state, and who leads it?
Name something the national government does and something our state or town does.
Americans have argued since 1787 about how much power belongs to the states. What are the main arguments on each side?
parts.do: Find out three things your town or county government does (roads, libraries, parks). Visit one, or look at its website together.

parts.title: Changing the Constitution
ask: Can the rules of the Constitution ever change? How?
Why did the framers make amending hard, but not impossible?
Pick one amendment that changed who could vote. What arguments won it, and how long did it take?
parts.do: Play 'amend the family constitution': propose one change and see if you can get three-fourths of the family to agree.

A.do: Make a small book of three family rules. Draw a picture for each and tell why it helps everyone.
rubric: Three rules, each with a picture

B.do: Make a poster with the three branches: who is in each, what each does, and one way each checks another.

C.t: A citizen's guide to the Bill of Rights
C.do: Make a pocket guide (a folded booklet) explaining each of the first ten amendments in plain words, with one example of each.

D.t: Federalist or Anti-Federalist? A position paper
D.do: Read one Federalist essay and one Anti-Federalist essay on the same question. Write 2-3 pages explaining both arguments fairly, then say which you find more persuasive and why.
rubric: Both arguments explained fairly and accurately
A reasoned judgment of your own

units.title: The Fifty States
units.blurb: Our own state, the regions, states and capitals, rivers and mountains, national parks, and how the country grew to fifty.

parts.title: Where We Live
ask: What is our address? What town, state and country do we live in?
What is our state's capital, and why do states have capitals?
How does where you live shape what you do every day?
parts.do: Make a set of nesting circles: your home in the middle, then town, county, state, country, continent and planet. Fill in each name.

parts.title: The Northeast and the Midwest
ask: Which states touch the Great Lakes?
Why did so many early cities grow in the Northeast?
How did the Midwest come to be called the nation's breadbasket?
parts.do: Cook a dish from each region this week (clam chowder, deep-dish pizza, a hotdish). Find each dish's state on the map.

parts.title: The South
ask: Which state is a peninsula?
What rivers flow through the South to the Gulf of Mexico?
How did the climate of the South shape what was grown there and how people lived?
parts.do: Trace the Mississippi River from Minnesota to the Gulf with your finger, naming the states on each side.

parts.title: The Mountain West and the Pacific
ask: Which states have the Rocky Mountains?
Why are Alaska and Hawaii drawn in boxes on many maps?
Why does the Continental Divide decide which ocean a raindrop reaches?
parts.do: Make a salt-dough relief map of the western states with the Rockies, the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades.

parts.title: National Parks and Landmarks
ask: Which national park would you most like to visit?
Why did the country decide to set aside land as parks?
Parks protect nature and welcome visitors. How do those two goals pull against each other?
parts.do: Plan a dream road trip to three national parks. Measure the route on the map and work out how many days of driving it would take.

parts.title: From Thirteen to Fifty
ask: How many states are there? Which state did you learn the most about?
Which were the first and last states to join?
Why did it take so long for some territories to become states?
parts.do: Make a fifty-states puzzle from a printed map glued to cardboard. Time how fast each person can put it together.

A.do: Make a small book about our state: its shape, its capital, its flag and one place you love. Draw a page for each.
rubric: Tells one thing about each page

B.do: Choose one state (not your own). Make a poster with its map, capital, flag, three landmarks and three interesting facts.

C.do: Make a chart or slide show comparing four regions: land, climate, cities, what people grow or make, and one landmark each.

D.do: Write a 2-3 page profile of one state: its physical geography, how and when it became a state, how its population and economy have changed, and a map you made.
rubric: A clear map and cited sources

units.title: The Harvard Classics
units.blurb: Six weeks of great books read aloud: Franklin, Homer, Darwin, Faraday, a sailor's voyage and the Declaration, with the skills to talk and write about them.

parts.title: Franklin's Autobiography
read: Harvard Classics: Franklin's Advice for the New Year
more: Harvard Classics: Franklin Learned the Secret
ask: Franklin made a list of good habits to practice. Which one would you pick?
Why did Franklin work on one habit a week instead of all at once?
Franklin admits he never reached his goal. Was the plan still worth it?
parts.do: Make a family habit chart in Franklin's style: each person picks one habit for the week and marks each day they keep it.

parts.title: Homer's Odyssey
read: Harvard Classics: Odysseus Silenced the Sirens
more: Harvard Classics: Odysseus Adrift on a Raft
ask: How did Odysseus get past the Sirens?
Why did he want to hear their song at all?
Odysseus planned ahead for his own weakness. When is that the wisest thing a person can do?
parts.do: Draw a map of the Odyssey on a big sheet, adding each place you hear about. Keep it for the whole unit.

parts.title: Darwin's Voyage of the Beagle
ask: What surprising animal did Darwin describe?
Darwin wrote down everything he saw. Why is a careful notebook so useful?
How do careful observations lead to big questions?
parts.do: Keep a naturalist's notebook for the week: each person sketches and describes one living thing a day, with the date and place.

parts.title: Faraday's Experiments
read: Harvard Classics: First Sparks of Electricity
ask: What can a magnet pick up? What can't it?
Faraday made electricity by moving a magnet near a wire. Why was that such a big discovery?
Faraday had little schooling and taught himself. What made him such a good scientist?
parts.do: Test what a magnet sticks to around the house and sort the things into two piles. Then build a circuit in the Circuit Builder.

parts.title: Two Years Before the Mast
read: Harvard Classics: A College Boy Goes to Sea
more: Harvard Classics: Home After Storms and Adventures
ask: What was hard about life on a sailing ship?
Why did Dana, a college student, choose to work as a common sailor?
Dana's book changed how people thought about sailors' lives. How can one honest account change minds?
parts.do: Learn three sailor's knots together and tie them on a rope rail between two chairs.

parts.title: The Declaration of Independence
read: Harvard Classics: Some Chose to Remain British Subjects
ask: What does 'independence' mean?
Which words from the Declaration do people quote most?
The Declaration is written as an argument. What does it set out to prove, and how?
parts.do: Read the opening two paragraphs aloud, each person taking a sentence. Copy one favorite line in your best handwriting.

A.do: Pick your favorite reading from the unit. Draw three pictures of what happened and tell it back to the family.
rubric: Says why it was a favorite

B.do: After each reading, write three sentences: what happened, what you learned, and a question you still have. Add a drawing for two of them.

C.do: Choose one author from the unit. Read a little more of their work and give a five-minute talk on who they were, what they wrote and why it lasted.

D.do: Write a 3-page essay comparing two readings from the unit on one theme (courage, curiosity, liberty, hard work). Quote both texts.
rubric: A clear thesis linking the two texts
Quotations explained, not just dropped in

units.title: The Human Body
units.blurb: The senses, bones and muscles, the heart and lungs, digestion, the brain and nerves, and how germs and the body's defenses work.

parts.title: Our Senses
ask: Which sense do you use to know a lemon is sour?
How do your senses work together when you eat?
Your brain sometimes fills in what your senses miss. How might that fool us?
parts.do: Set up a senses table: a blindfold tasting of five safe foods, a 'mystery bag' to feel, and sounds to guess with eyes closed.

parts.title: Bones and Muscles
ask: Feel the bones in your hand. How many can you find?
Why do muscles work in pairs?
Bones are alive and change all your life. What helps keep them strong?
