parts.do: Trace a family member on a big sheet of paper and draw in the main bones. Label the skull, ribs, spine, arm and leg bones.

parts.title: The Heart and Lungs
more: Harvard Classics: Pulse Aids Epochal Discoveries
ask: Put your hand on your chest. What do you feel, and what is it doing?
Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
William Harvey showed in 1628 that blood goes around in a circle. How did he reason it out without modern tools?
parts.do: Count pulses for 15 seconds at rest, then after a minute of jumping jacks. Multiply by four and make a family bar graph.

parts.title: Digestion
ask: Where does your food go after you swallow it?
Why do we chew? What does saliva do?
The small intestine is long and folded. Why would more surface help?
parts.do: Model digestion: mash a cracker in a zip bag with a little water (the stomach), then squeeze it through an old stocking (the intestines).

parts.title: Brain and Nerves
ask: What does your brain do while you sleep?
Catch a falling ruler. How fast did your nerves send the message?
Why are some actions, like pulling your hand from a hot stove, done before you even think?
parts.do: Ruler-drop test: one person drops a ruler, the other catches it. Record the distance and use a chart to turn it into reaction time.

parts.title: Germs and Defenses
read: Harvard Classics: He Introduced the Germ
ask: Why do we wash our hands before we eat?
How does the body fight germs that get inside?
Before Pasteur, many doctors didn't believe tiny living things caused disease. What evidence changed their minds?
parts.do: Glitter germs: put a pinch of glitter on one person's hands, then shake hands around the family. See how far it spreads, then see how well soap and water get it off.

A.do: On your traced body outline, glue paper shapes for the heart, lungs, stomach and brain. Point to each and say what it does.
rubric: Four organs in about the right places
Finished and shown to the family

B.do: Make a six-page booklet, one page per system from the unit (senses, bones, muscles, heart and lungs, digestion, nerves), with a drawing and three facts each.

C.do: Make a poster or slide show following one bite of food, or one breath of air, through the body, showing every system it touches.
rubric: Follows the path in the right order
Explains how the systems depend on each other

D.t: A lab report on exercise and heart rate
D.do: Measure heart rate before and after three levels of exercise for several family members. Write a report with a hypothesis, data table, graph, and an explanation using what you learned about circulation and feedback.
rubric: Data in a table and graph

units.title: The Seasons
units.blurb: Why Earth has seasons, a tree adopted for the year, birds and animals getting ready for winter, the sky's calendar, and a nature journal.

parts.title: Why We Have Seasons
read: Sun, Moon and Stars: Day and night, and the seasons
more: Why We Have Seasons in Earth Science
Handbook of Nature Study: The Sun and the Earth
ask: What are the four seasons, and which one are we in now?
Earth is a little closer to the Sun in January. So why is January cold in the United States?
How does the tilt of Earth's axis change both the length of the day and how strongly sunlight hits the ground?
parts.do: In a dark room, carry a globe (or a ball with a pencil through it) around a lamp. Keep the pencil leaning the same way the whole time, and watch which half gets more light at each side of the circle.

parts.title: Adopt a Tree
read: Handbook of Nature Study: Adopting a tree for a year
ask: What does our tree look like today? What color are its leaves?
Why do many trees drop their leaves in fall while pines keep their needles?
A leaf turns yellow or red when the tree stops making green chlorophyll. Why would a tree stop making it before winter?
parts.do: Pick one tree near home to visit all through this unit. Measure around its trunk with a string, make a bark rubbing, and press one leaf. Start a family nature journal with a page for the tree.

parts.title: Getting Ready for Winter
more: Handbook of Nature Study: Birds' nests in winter
ask: Where do bugs, frogs and bears go in winter?
Some birds fly south and some stay all winter. How do the ones that stay find food and keep warm?
Hibernating, migrating and staying active are three ways to get through winter. What does each one cost an animal, and what does it gain?
parts.do: Make a simple bird feeder from a pine cone, peanut butter (or shortening) and birdseed. Hang it where you can see it from a window and keep a tally of the birds that visit.

parts.title: Weather Through the Year
read: Home Geography: Dew, frost, clouds, fog, rain, hail and snow
more: Handbook of Nature Study: Water forms: vapor, dew, frost and snow
ask: What kind of weather do we get in each season where we live?
What is the difference between weather and climate?
Places near the equator have hardly any winter, and places near the poles have months of dark. Use Earth's tilt to explain both.
parts.do: Keep a family weather chart for the week: the temperature at the same time each day, the sky, and the wind. At the end of the week, make a bar graph of the temperatures.

parts.title: The Sky's Calendar
read: Handbook of Nature Study: How to make a sundial
more: McGuffey's Third Reader: The Clock and the Sun-Dial
ask: Where does the Sun come up in the morning, and where does it go down?
Why is your noon shadow short in summer and long in winter?
Before clocks and printed calendars, how could people use the Sun and Moon to know the time of year?
parts.do: Stand a stick in the ground (or tape a pencil upright on a sunny windowsill). Mark the tip of its shadow every hour on a sunny day. Then measure the noon shadow once a week for the rest of the unit.

parts.title: Poems of the Seasons
read: Home Geography: The signs of the seasons
ask: Which season is your favorite, and what do you see, hear and smell in it?
Poets often use the seasons to stand for something else, like spring for a new start. Can you find an example?
Shelley asked, 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?' What was he really saying, and do you agree?
parts.do: Read your nature journal pages together. Each person picks one page and turns it into a short poem or a picture with a caption. Share them at a family poetry tea.

A.do: Fold a paper into four boxes, one for each season. Draw your adopted tree as it looks now, then draw how you think it looks in the other three seasons. Tell a grown-up one thing about each box to write underneath.
rubric: Four boxes, one for each season
Each picture shows a real change (leaves, buds, snow, fruit)
Can tell one fact about each season

B.do: Make a four-page field guide to this season where you live: one page of trees, one of birds or animals, one of weather, one of the sky. Draw each thing and write two true sentences about it.
rubric: Four pages with drawings from real observation
Two true sentences on each page
At least one measurement (temperature, shadow or trunk size)
Neat writing with capitals and end marks

C.do: Use the noon shadow you measured each week, plus sunrise and sunset times from a newspaper or almanac, to make two line graphs. Write one page explaining what the graphs show and how Earth's tilt causes it.
rubric: Two clearly labeled graphs from real data
The explanation uses tilt, not distance from the Sun
At least three measurements on each graph

D.do: Ask one question about the season (for example: does the noon Sun's height match the angle the ladder predicts for our latitude, or how does leaf color change on one tree week by week?). Collect data for at least three weeks, compare it with what the lessons predict, and write a two-page report.
rubric: Data collected on at least three dates and shown in a table or graph
Compares results with the expected values and explains any difference

units.title: The Solar System
units.blurb: Day and night, the Moon and its phases, the Sun, the planets near and far, comets and meteors, and the stars beyond.

parts.title: Day, Night and the Seasons
read: Sun, Moon, and Stars: Day and night, and the seasons
more: Day and night in Earth Science
ask: Why is it dark at night?
Why is summer warmer than winter, if Earth isn't much closer to the Sun?
How would the seasons be different if Earth weren't tilted?
parts.do: In a dark room, shine a flashlight 'Sun' on a globe. Turn the globe slowly to make day and night, then walk it around the light with the tilt kept the same.

parts.title: The Moon
read: Sun, Moon, and Stars: A pretend trip to the Moon
ask: Does the Moon really change shape?
Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
What causes a solar eclipse, and why don't we have one every month?
parts.do: Draw the Moon every clear night of the unit, at about the same time. Then make the phases with an orange (the Moon), a lamp and your head (Earth).

parts.title: The Sun
read: Sun, Moon, and Stars: The head of our family: the Sun
ask: Why do we never look straight at the Sun?
How does the Sun make its light and heat?
The Sun is an ordinary star. Why does it look so different from the others?
parts.do: Make a shadow clock: stand a stick in the ground and mark the end of its shadow every hour. Measure the shadows and see when it was shortest.

parts.title: The Planets
read: Sun, Moon, and Stars: The giant planets, and a model you can walk
ask: Which planet is the biggest? Which is closest to the Sun?
Why are the inner planets rocky and the outer ones giant balls of gas?
A real-scale model of the solar system won't fit in a book. Why is it so hard to picture its size?
parts.do: Walk a scale model: the Sun is a ball at your front door, and you pace out each planet's distance down the street using a printed scale.

parts.title: Comets and Meteors
read: Sun, Moon, and Stars: Visitors: the comets
ask: What is a shooting star really?
Why does a comet's tail point away from the Sun?
Some meteorites are older than any rock on Earth. What can they tell us?
parts.do: Make a comet from a ball of foil with paper streamer tails. Run with it past a 'Sun' lamp and turn so the tail always points away from it.

parts.title: Stars and Beyond
read: Nature Study: The two Dippers and the Pole-star
more: Harvard Classics: Star Gazing, a Cure for Tired Minds
ask: Can you find the Big Dipper?
How do sailors use the North Star?
The light from some stars left them thousands of years ago. What does that mean when we look at them?
parts.do: On a clear night, go out together and find the Big Dipper and the North Star. Draw what you see, then try to find one more constellation.

A.do: Make a mobile of the Sun and eight planets from paper circles of different sizes, in the right order. Name them as you hang them up.

B.do: Keep a Moon journal for four weeks: a drawing and the date each clear night, then a page explaining the phases.
rubric: A clear explanation of why phases happen

C.t: A scale model of the solar system
C.do: Work out a scale for the planets' sizes and distances. Build or draw a model to that scale, and write up your math.
rubric: Sizes and distances follow the scale
Explains why sizes and distances need different scales

D.do: Measure the Sun's noon shadow on several days, or time the Moon's rising over a week. Write a lab report connecting your data to Earth's motion, with a graph.
rubric: Data in a table and graph

units.title: Weather
units.blurb: The air around us, the water cycle, clouds and rain, wind and pressure, storms, and how forecasters read the sky.

parts.title: The Air Around Us
read: Fairy-Land of Science: We live at the bottom of an ocean of air
ask: Can you feel air? How do you know it's there?
Air presses on us all the time. Why don't we feel squashed?
Why does air get thinner as you climb a mountain?
parts.do: Fill a glass to the brim with water, cover it with a card, and turn it over above a sink. Talk about what holds the card on.

parts.title: The Water Cycle
more: Fairy-Land of Science: A drop of water goes up into the sky
ask: Where does a puddle go when it dries up?
Tell the story of one drop of water through the whole water cycle.
The same water has gone around and around for billions of years. What powers the cycle?
parts.do: Make a water cycle in a bag: a little water with blue coloring in a zip bag taped to a sunny window. Check it each morning and draw what you see.

parts.title: Clouds and Rain
read: Home Geography: Dew, frost, clouds, fog, rain, hail and snow
ask: What shapes do you see in the clouds today?
Why do clouds form high up and not at the ground?
Why does one side of a mountain range get lots of rain and the other side very little?
parts.do: Keep a family cloud log: twice a day, look up, sketch the clouds and name the type. Did that kind of cloud bring rain later?

parts.title: Wind
more: Fairy-Land of Science: Air pushes up, weighing the air, and the wind
ask: How can we tell which way the wind is blowing?
Why does a breeze blow in from the sea on a hot afternoon?
Why do winds curve instead of blowing straight from high pressure to low?
parts.do: Make a wind vane from a straw, a pin, a pencil eraser and a paper arrow. Mark north, south, east and west on its base and read it each day.

parts.title: Storms
ask: What makes thunder?
Count the seconds between a flash and its thunder. What does the number tell you?
How do forecasters warn people about a hurricane days ahead but a tornado only minutes ahead?
parts.do: Next time there is a storm, watch from indoors: count seconds from flash to thunder and divide by five to estimate the miles to the lightning.

parts.title: Forecasting
read: Nature Study: How to read weather maps
more: Forecasting tools in Weather and Climate
ask: What will the weather be tomorrow? How could we guess?
What tools do weather watchers use?
A forecast says 40 percent chance of rain. What does that mean, and what doesn't it mean?
parts.do: Run a family weather station for the week: a thermometer, a rain gauge from a straight-sided jar, and your wind vane. Make a forecast each night and check it in the morning.

A.do: Keep a picture weather chart for one week: draw sun, clouds, rain or wind each day. At the end, count which weather came most.

B.do: Record temperature, rain and wind each day for two weeks. Make a bar graph of temperature and write three things you noticed.

C.do: Record weather for two weeks and make your own forecast each evening. Present a two-minute weather report on video or live, and score how often your forecasts were right.
rubric: Forecasts use real clues (clouds, pressure, wind)
Honest scoring of hits and misses

D.do: Choose one kind of storm. Write a 2-3 page report on how it forms, how it is forecast, and one historic example before 2000, with a diagram and cited sources.
rubric: Accurate explanation of how it forms
A historic example with facts and dates

units.title: Westward Expansion
units.blurb: The Louisiana Purchase, Lewis and Clark, pioneers on the trails, the Gold Rush, the railroad, and the Native nations whose lands it crossed.

parts.title: The Louisiana Purchase
ask: What did Lewis and Clark set out to find?
In 1803 the United States bought a huge territory from France. Why did both sides want the deal?
Jefferson wasn't sure the Constitution allowed the purchase, but he made it anyway. Was that the right call?
parts.do: On a blank map of the United States, color the land of the Louisiana Purchase. Then trace the route of Lewis and Clark up the Missouri River to the Pacific.

parts.title: Explorers and Mapmakers
ask: How can you tell which way is north?
Lewis and Clark had no maps of the West. How did they make their own?
Sacagawea and many Native guides helped the expedition. What did they know that the explorers didn't?
parts.do: Go outside with a compass. Make a map of your yard or a park, with a key, a compass rose and paces for distance.

parts.title: Pioneers on the Trail
more: Westward Expansion in U.S. History I
ask: What did pioneer families pack in their wagons?
Why would a family leave everything they knew to go west?
'Manifest destiny' was a popular idea in the 1840s. What did it claim, and who disagreed with it?
parts.do: Pack a pretend wagon: a space the size of a big blanket. Choose what to bring for a six-month trip, and weigh the pile on a bathroom scale.

parts.title: Gold Rush
read: Harvard Classics: Just Before the Gold Rush
ask: Why did so many people rush to California in 1849?
Who got rich in the Gold Rush, the miners or the people who sold them supplies?
California grew so fast it became a state by 1850. What problems does very fast growth bring?
parts.do: Pan for 'gold': hide painted pebbles in a tub of sand and water and pan with pie tins. Then set prices for a store and see who earns more, the miner or the shopkeeper.

parts.title: Native Nations of the West
ask: How did Plains peoples use the buffalo?
How did settlers and the railroad change life for Native nations?
Treaties were made and often broken. How should a nation keep its promises, and what happens to trust when it doesn't?
parts.do: Learn about the Native nation that lived where your home is now. Find its name on a map and one thing about its way of life, then share it at dinner.

parts.title: The Railroad Ties It Together
ask: How long did it take to cross the country by wagon, and how long by train?
Who built the railroad, and what was the work like?
The railroad helped the country grow and also ended the open range. How do we weigh a change that helps some and harms others?
parts.do: Lay a 'railroad' of masking tape across the house from east to west, with a station for each part of the unit. Walk it and tell the story of the West in order.

A.do: Build a covered wagon from a small box, paper and straws. Put three tiny things in it a pioneer family would need, and say why.
rubric: The wagon has a cover and wheels
Three things a pioneer would need

B.do: Write five diary entries as a child on the Oregon Trail: leaving home, crossing a river, a hard day, meeting new people, arriving. Add a map of the route.
rubric: Real places and dangers of the trail
Clear sentences, capitals and end marks

C.do: Make a large map showing how the United States grew from 1783 to 1853, with each addition dated and colored, and a short paragraph on how each was gained.
rubric: All the main additions shown and dated

D.do: Write a 2-3 page essay on westward expansion from three points of view (a settler family, a Native nation, a railroad worker), using primary or secondary sources for each.
